children.name: Poikilocarbo
children.description: Red-legged cormorant — a monotypic genus found along the Pacific coast of South America from northern Peru to Tierra del Fuego. Easily distinguished from all other cormorants by its vivid coral-red legs and feet, which contrast sharply with its grey-blue plumage and orange throat patch. The red-legged cormorant is a specialist of exposed rocky shores and strong tidal currents, where it forages in the surf zone among breaking waves.

children.name: Poikilocarbo gaimardi
children.description: The red-legged cormorant (Poikilocarbo gaimardi), also known as the red-legged shag, red-footed cormorant, red-footed shag, Gaimard's cormorant and grey cormorant, is a species of cormorant resident to the coastline of South America. It is the only member of the genus Poikilocarbo. It is non-colonial unlike most seabirds. The red-legged cormorant has not been observed wing-spreading, which is unusual among cormorant species.

children.name: Urile
children.description: North Pacific cormorants — a genus of four species that breed on the cold coasts and islands of the northern Pacific Rim, from Japan and Kamchatka across the Aleutians to western North America. They have distinctive bare facial skin patterns and, in most species, a bright blue or purple gape. One species, the spectacled cormorant, is the only cormorant to have gone extinct in historical times, vanishing from the Commander Islands around 1850.

children.name: Urile penicillatus
children.description: Brandt's cormorant (Urile penicillatus) is a strictly marine bird of the cormorant family of seabirds that inhabits the Pacific coast of North America. It ranges, in the summer, from Alaska to the Gulf of California, but the population north of Vancouver Island migrates south during the winter. Its specific name, penicillatus is Latin for a painter's brush (pencil of hairs), in reference to white plumes on its neck and back during the early breeding season. The common name honors the German naturalist Johann Friedrich von Brandt of the Academy of Sciences at St. Petersburg, who described the species from specimens collected on expeditions to the Pacific during the early 19th century.

children.name: Urile urile
children.description:
The red-faced cormorant (Urile urile), red-faced shag or violet shag, is a bird species of the family Phalacrocoracidae.
Its range spans from the eastern tip of Hokkaidō in Japan, northern korean peninsula, via the Kuril Islands, the southern tip of the Kamchatka Peninsula and the Aleutian Arc to the Alaska Peninsula and Gulf of Alaska.

children.name: Urile pelagicus
children.description: The pelagic cormorant (Urile pelagicus), also known as Baird's cormorant or violet-green cormorant, is a small member of the cormorant family Phalacrocoracidae.

children.name: Urile perspicillatus
children.description: The spectacled cormorant or Pallas's cormorant (Urile perspicillatus) is an extinct marine bird of the cormorant family of seabirds that inhabited Bering Island and possibly other places in the Commander Islands and the nearby coast of Kamchatka in the far northeast of Russia.

children.name: Gulosus
children.description: European shag — a monotypic genus separated from Phalacrocorax by molecular studies, restricted to the temperate and boreal coastal waters of Europe and North Africa. The European shag is distinguished from the great cormorant by its smaller size, more slender build, iridescent green-black plumage, and a distinctive forward-curling crest in breeding plumage. Unlike the great cormorant, it is strictly a marine species that rarely if ever ventures onto fresh water.

children.name: Gulosus aristotelis
children.description: The European shag or common shag (Gulosus aristotelis) is a species of cormorant.

children.name: Nannopterum
children.description: American cormorants — a genus of three species restricted to the Americas, including the only flightless cormorant in the world. These cormorants have undergone rapid evolutionary diversification in the New World, from the Galápagos flightless cormorant to the widespread double-crested and neotropic cormorants. The genus was long lumped into Phalacrocorax but molecular studies confirm its distinctness, with the flightless cormorant representing an extreme adaptation to an island environment without terrestrial predators.

children.name: Nannopterum harrisi
children.description: The flightless cormorant (Nannopterum harrisi), also known as the Galápagos cormorant, is a cormorant endemic to the Galápagos Islands, and an example of the highly unusual fauna there.

children.name: Nannopterum auritum
children.description: The double-crested cormorant (Nannopterum auritum) is a member of the cormorant family of water birds. It is found near rivers and lakes and in coastal areas and is widely distributed across North America, from the Aleutian Islands in Alaska down to Florida and Mexico. Measuring in length, it is entirely black except for a bare patch of orange-yellow facial skin and some extra plumage that it exhibits in the breeding season when it grows a double crest in which black feathers are mingled with white. Five subspecies are recognized. It mainly eats fish and hunts by swimming and diving. Its feathers, like all cormorants, are not waterproof, and it must dry them out after spending time in the water. Once threatened by the use of DDT, the numbers of this bird have increased markedly in recent years.

children.name: Leucocarbo
children.description: Blue-eyed shags — a southern-hemisphere genus of medium to large cormorants found around the Antarctic and subantarctic islands, the southern coasts of South America, and New Zealand. They are named for the vivid blue ring around the eye that most species display, a feature unique among cormorants. Many Leucocarbo species have extremely restricted ranges, confined to single island groups, making them among the most range-restricted of all seabirds and particularly vulnerable to introduced predators.

children.name: Leucocarbo bougainvilliorum
children.description: The guanay cormorant or guanay shag (Leucocarbo bougainvilliorum) is a member of the cormorant family found on the Pacific coast of Peru and northern Chile.

children.name: Leucocarbo ranfurlyi
children.description: The Bounty shag (Leucocarbo ranfurlyi), also known as the Bounty Island shag, is a species of cormorant of the family Phalacrocoracidae.

children.name: Leucocarbo carunculatus
children.description: The New Zealand king shag (Leucocarbo carunculatus), also known as the rough-faced shag, king shag or kawau pāteketeke, is a rare bird endemic to New Zealand. Some taxonomic authorities, including the International Ornithologists' Union, place this species in the genus Leucocarbo. Others place it in the genus Phalacrocorax.

children.name: Leucocarbo onslowi
children.description:
The Chatham Islands shag (Leucocarbo onslowi), also known as the Chatham shag, is a species of bird in the cormorant and shag family, Phalacrocoracidae. It is endemic to the Chatham Islands of New Zealand. For a long time the species was placed in the genus Phalacrocorax; today it is mostly placed with the other blue-eyed shags of New Zealand and Antarctica in the genus Leucocarbo. Its closest relative is the Otago shag of South Island.
This is a large, pied shag with a long crest. It is highly coastal, rarely foraging far from shore, although sometimes feeds in the large and brackish Te Whanga Lagoon. It forages for fish and cephalopods and roosts on rocky shores. The species is colonial, breeding in small colonies around the Chatham Islands. Little is known about its breeding behaviour. The species is threatened by introduced predators, disturbance at its breeding colonies and habitat loss.

children.name: Leucocarbo chalconotus
children.description: The Stewart Island shag (Leucocarbo chalconotus;) is a species of shag found on New Zealand's South Island and Stewart Island. The Stewart Island shag has sometimes been split into two species, the Foveaux shag and the Otago shag.

children.name: Leucocarbo colensoi
children.description: The Auckland shag or Auckland Islands shag (Leucocarbo colensoi) is a species of cormorant from New Zealand.

children.name: Leucocarbo campbelli
children.description: The Campbell shag (Leucocarbo campbelli), also known as the Campbell Island shag, is a species of bird in the family Phalacrocoracidae.
children.namedAfter: Campbell Island (named after Captain John Campbell)

children.name: Leucocarbo atriceps
children.description: The imperial shag or imperial cormorant (Leucocarbo atriceps) is a black-and-white cormorant native to southern South America, islands of the Subantarctic, and the Antarctic Peninsula, primarily in rocky coastal regions, but locally also at large inland lakes.

children.name: Leucocarbo georgianus
children.description: The South Georgia shag (Leucocarbo georgianus), also known as the South Georgia cormorant, is a marine cormorant native to South Georgia and a few other subantarctic islands in the South Atlantic Ocean.

children.name: Leucocarbo melanogenis
children.description: The Crozet shag (Leucocarbo melanogenis), also known as the South Georgia cormorant, is a marine cormorant native to the Crozet, Prince Edward and Marion islands in the South Atlantic Ocean.

children.name: Leucocarbo bransfieldensis
children.description: The Antarctic shag (Leucocarbo bransfieldensis), sometimes referred to as the imperial cormorant, king cormorant, imperial shag, blue-eyed shag or Antarctic cormorant, is the only species of the cormorant family found in the Antarctic.

children.name: Leucocarbo verrucosus
children.description: The Kerguelen shag (Leucocarbo verrucosus) is a species of cormorant endemic to the Kerguelen Islands in the southern Indian Ocean, one of the most isolated places on Earth.

children.name: Leucocarbo nivalis
children.description: The Heard Island shag (Leucocarbo nivalis), or Heard Island cormorant, is a marine cormorant native to the Australian territory comprising the Heard and McDonald Islands in the Southern Ocean, which is about 4,100 km south-west of Perth, Western Australia.

children.name: Leucocarbo purpurascens
children.description: The Macquarie shag (Leucocarbo purpurascens), Macquarie Island shag or Macquarie Island cormorant, is a marine cormorant native to Macquarie Island in the Southern Ocean, about halfway between Australia and Antarctica.
